THE WORDS FOR A BIKE

CHAPTER 1 · THE SHOP
THE TERMS
Shona wheels it to the counter. "Two days, forty pounds. Back by six tomorrow or it's a third day, and that's twenty more. Hundred deposit, cash."
Your train home leaves at eight tomorrow evening; you were planning to ride in at seven.
What does riding in at seven cost you?
Shona said "back by six tomorrow or it's a third day", and a third day is "twenty more". Seven is after six.
WHICH BIKE
"Forty miles on a charge, and the loop is sixty-six. I'd not take the e-bike if I were you. The yellow one's lighter and it doesn't run out."
Shona taps the e-bike's battery: the charge light is green, fully charged, right now.
Which bike is she telling you to take, and why?
"I'd not take the e-bike if I were you" is advice against it: "forty miles on a charge" is short of the loop's sixty-six.
KNEE JUST BENT
She stands you astride it, phone ready for the wall. "Knee just bent at the bottom. Flick the lever under the saddle and slide it up an inch."
The saddle sits on a tube that slides into the frame; a small lever clamps it.
What does Shona want you to slide up?
The SEAT POST carries the saddle and slides down into the SEAT TUBE, the frame tube that holds it. A "rod" is a translation.
THE RIGHT LEVER
Her hands over yours. "Right one's the front brake here, not like at home. Grab that alone on a hill and you're over the handlebars. Squeeze both."
Two blades under your fingers, one each side of the handlebars; you squeeze them towards you.
What is she telling you to squeeze, both at once?
BRAKE LEVERS: a lever pivots when you squeeze it. "Handles" and "grips" are translations; the GRIPS are the rubber ends of the handlebars.
THE WEE ARM
Shona clicks the shifter and turns the pedal. "Watch the back wheel. That wee arm's what moves the chain across the cogs. Bend it and you're walking."
A sprung arm under the cogs on the back wheel, with two tiny wheels inside it.
What is the arm that moves the chain called?
The DERAILLEUR is the arm that pushes the chain sideways. The CASSETTE is the stack of cogs it crosses; the CHAINRINGS sit at the pedals.
LORRIES AND NO VERGE
Outside, she points down the river. "Out through Dores, loch on your right, and keep it there all the way round. Not the A82. Lorries, and no verge."
Two roads leave town: over the bridge to Dores, or straight down onto the A82.
Which road, and which side is the water on?
"Out through Dores" is the road over the bridge, and the loch stays "on your right". "Not the A82" rules the other road out.
ROUTE CHOICE 1 · DORES
THE FORK AT DORES
Dores beach, late morning, the water flat and grey. Above the shingle the road splits: along the shore, or up over the moor. Both end at Fort Augustus.
SHORE ROAD
ALONG THE WATER
By the water, a waterfall, a café, one steep climb out of Foyers.
HIGH ROAD
UP OVER THE MOOR
Sheep, cattle grids, one farm and no shop; a long descent at the end.
CHAPTER 2 · THE SHORE ROAD
FLAT BY THE WATER
Two miles past Dores the back of the bike goes soft and wanders. You stop by the water. A thorn stands out of the rubber like a nail.
The outer rubber that meets the road, not the soft tube inside; the thorn is there.
You ring the shop. "Shona, there's a thorn in ___."
The thorn is in the TYRE, the outer rubber. The INNER TUBE is the soft ring that holds the air, and the RIM is metal.
TWO PLASTIC HOOKS
In the saddlebag: a spare tube, a mini pump, and two flat plastic hooks. You have never used them. You know exactly what they are for.
Slide one under the tyre's edge, hook it on a spoke, work the other along.
What are the two plastic hooks called?
TYRE LEVERS lever the tyre over the rim; "lifters" is a translation. A SPOKE KEY is a tiny spanner that tightens spokes.
THE ORANGE JERSEY
A rider in an orange jersey slows beside you, thumbs your back tyre. "Forty? You'll pinch that on the first pothole past Foyers. Sixty-five, at least. Cheerio."
The pump got heavy at forty, so you stopped. A pinch: the rim cuts the tube.
What is he warning will happen at forty?
"You'll pinch that on the first pothole": the rim cuts the tube when the tyre is soft. Another flat, not a burst.
THE CLIMB OUT OF FOYERS
The climb out of Foyers is a wall. You stand on the pedals, click for an easier gear, and your feet spin on nothing. The chain hangs loose.
The chain dangles below the big ring at the pedals; its teeth are bare.
You ring the shop. What has happened?
The verb is COMES OFF: the chain leaves the CHAINRING and hangs. "Fallen" and "gone out" are translated, and nobody on a bike says them.
CHAPTER 2 · THE HIGH ROAD
THE CATTLE GRID
The high road: sheep, a cattle grid you hit too fast, and then a wobble in the front wheel, side to side, that was not there before.
One thin wire between the hub and the rim is slack; it twangs like a string.
What has the cattle grid loosened?
A SPOKE is a wire under tension; one slack and the RIM wobbles. The HUB is the centre, and "radius" is a translation.
SIXTY ON THE BACK
Whitebridge. The tyres squash like porridge. You text Shona a photo of the mini pump on the valve. Back in seconds: "Sixty on the back. All of it."
A hundred strokes on the pump gets you there; the tyre goes hard under your thumb.
What is she telling you to do to the back tyre?
PUMP UP is the verb and the number follows TO. "Until" wants an event, not a figure; "at sixty" is a translation.
THE FARMER'S GATE
A farmer on a quad bike holds the gate. "Four miles down to Fort Augustus and it's all brakes. The café at the top's your last. Mind yourself."
The red quad bike idles at the gate. Your bottle is empty; the road drops away.
What is the farmer telling you, in plain words?
"The café at the top's your last" means no more café below, and "all brakes" says the road drops. Get what you need here.
THE LONG DRAG
The drag after Whitebridge. You push on the pedals and the back end lurches: the chain lets go of its cog under your weight, catches, lets go again.
It only happens under load; soft pedalling on the flat, the stack of cogs is fine.
You text Shona. The gears keep doing what?
Gears SLIP: the chain loses its grip on the cog under load. "Sliding" and "escaping" are translations, and a worn CASSETTE is the usual cause.
CHAPTER 3 · FORT AUGUSTUS
DUTCH, THEN DANISH
Moira, into her pint: "Dutch. No - Danish. You've the look." You: "Swiss." Jean, from the other stool: "Whereabouts? The German bit or the French bit?"
Moira's pint glass sits under the lamp; Jean has not looked up from her half.
What is Jean asking you for?
"Whereabouts" asks for the place inside the country; "the German bit or the French bit" are regions of Switzerland, not languages.
FLAT AS A PLATE
Moira: "The bay at first light, flat calm. Twice I've seen her." Jean: "Off the castle, the back of six, if you must. Calm, or nothing."
The loch out the window lies flat as a plate. Back of six: just past six.
What do the two women actually agree on?
Moira says "first light" and "flat calm"; Jean says "back of six" and "calm, or nothing". Same time, same water; only the place differs.
JEAN AND THE MULTI-TOOL
Jean heard it from the bar. Outside she spins the back wheel: a whisper every turn. "Rubbing. Two minutes." A multi-tool from her coat. "Archie. The pier, six."
Two rubber blocks either side of the rim, and one is touching. Archie has a boat.
What does Jean say is rubbing?
BRAKE PADS are the rubber blocks that grip the rim; one out of line rubs. LEVERS are at your hands, CABLES only pull.
ROUTE CHOICE 2 · THE PIER
SIX AT THE PIER
Six, and the loch is a mirror. Archie MacRae waits in a wooden launch, lamp lit. "The castle, deep water. Or the bay, shallow. You pay the diesel."
THE CASTLE
OUT TO THE CASTLE
An hour up the loch; deep water, the sonar ground, and rules aboard.
THE BAY
DRIFT INTO THE BAY
Ten minutes out, engine off, weed and birds; you keep your mouth shut.
CHAPTER 4 · THE CASTLE
RULES ABOARD
Archie's hand on the tiller. "Rules. Sit low. Nobody stands, nobody shouts. Camera stays below the rail till I say. She hears a boat before she sees it."
The rail is the boat's wooden edge; his hand on the tiller has not moved.
When does the camera come above the rail?
"Camera stays below the rail till I say": the signal is his word, not her appearing. Sitting low is a separate rule.
THE ORANGE STRAP
The bike lies in the bow. Archie throws you a strap. "Round the frame over the back wheel, where your bags hang. Not the thin bit. It'll tear."
An orange strap over the metal frame above the back wheel, where the bags clip on.
What is Archie telling you to strap it by?
The PANNIER RACK holds the bags and takes a strap. A MUDGUARD is thin and tears; a CHAIN GUARD sits at the pedals.
NOT THIS ONE
Fifty yards off, a wet back and a wake. Archie, barely audible: "She'll go down. She'll come up once more, further off. That's your picture. Not this one."
The castle on its rock behind her; the white wake is already moving away from you.
When does Archie want you to take the photo?
"She'll come up once more, further off. That's your picture. Not this one": wait for the next surfacing, even though it is further away.
CHAPTER 4 · THE BAY
ENGINE OFF
Archie cuts the engine and the bay goes silent. "Nobody talks now. If the birds lift, you look where they came from, not where they're going."
Thirty gulls sit on the water off the reeds; the launch drifts, and nobody has spoken.
The gulls all lift at once. Where do you look?
"Look where they came from, not where they're going": the birds flee something, so the something is under the spot they left.
TEN SECONDS
The bike won't fit past the thwart with the front wheel on. Archie nods at the small lever at the hub. "Flip that. Wheel's off in ten seconds."
The front wheel leans on the thwart, the bench across the boat, its lever flipped open.
What did you do to get the wheel off?
The QUICK RELEASE is the cam lever that clamps the wheel into the FORK, and you UNDO it. "Quick lock" and "fast lever" are translations.
COUNT TO TWENTY
A wake crosses the bay, nothing in front of it. A neck lifts against the sunrise. Archie, under his breath: "Count. Over twenty seconds up, that's no seal."
You count under your breath. At nineteen the neck is still up; at twenty-four it goes.
What does your count tell you it was?
"Over twenty seconds up, that's no seal": it went at twenty-four, so by Archie's rule it is something else. What, he does not say.
CHAPTER 5 · THE NORTH SIDE
TICK, TICK
Archie puts you off below the castle. On the walkers' path, something ticks once a turn at the back wheel, like a card in the spokes.
The curved strip over the back wheel that keeps spray off your back has bent inwards.
What has bent in? You'll need the word for Shona.
A MUDGUARD stops the wheel throwing water up your back; bent in, it touches the tyre. A REFLECTOR is flat and only shines back light.
THE COUNT
Shona runs a thumb down the sheet. "Scratch on the top tube - that was on already. Mudguard's new, fifteen. Kit's all there." She counts notes out.
A hundred went down in cash on Wednesday. It is ten past twelve on Thursday.
How much comes back across the counter?
"That was on already" means the scratch is not yours; "new, fifteen" is the only charge. A hundred less fifteen is eighty-five.
ON THE WALL
THAT'S HER

Shona zooms in on the third photo and says nothing for a long time. "That's her." She pins it on the wall, next to the one of you astride the yellow bike, and hands over eighty-five pounds. Train at eight.
LOOP COMPLETE
AYE, THAT'S THE LOCH
The third photo is a wake and rain on the lens. Shona looks at it properly, which is something. "Aye, that's the loch." Eighty-five pounds back, legs that will hurt tomorrow, and a train at eight.
PHOTOS MISSING
THE PICTURE NOT TAKEN

The loop is done and the phone was in the bag when it mattered. Shona hands the deposit back and asks what you saw. You tell her: the back, the wake, the neck. She has heard it before. She nods anyway.
OUT OF CHANCES
HOME ON THE BUS
The bike comes home on the rack of the bus from Fort Augustus, you in the seat behind it. Shona counts the kit and does not ask. Out of the window the loch keeps herself to herself.
